Noun A noun is a naming word: it names a person, a place, a thing or an idea. In plain words. A noun is simply a name for something. It can name a person ( Peter , mother ), a place ( Jerusalem , garden ), a thing ( bread , cross ) or something you cannot touch at all ( love , grace , faith ). A quick test: if you can put “the” or “a” in front of it, it is very likely a noun. An everyday example. “The baker sold fresh bread in the village .” Baker, bread and village are all nouns. So is the word kindness in “Her kindness surprised us.” Why it matters when you read the Bible. Many of the Bible’s richest words are nouns: grace , righteousness , redemption , covenant . When a verse turns on a noun, slow down and ask what that noun means elsewhere in Scripture. Notice too that Scripture gives Christ many nouns as titles: the Word, the Lamb, the Shepherd, the Vine. Each name tells you something true about who he is and what he does for his people. John 1:1 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. John calls Jesus by a noun, “the Word”. Just as our words show what is in our mind, the Son makes God known (see John 1:18). Romans 6:23 For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. Look at the nouns: wages and gift. Wages are earned; a gift is not. The whole gospel sits in the contrast between those two nouns. Noticing the key nouns in a verse is often the quickest way to see what it is about.

Pronoun A pronoun is a short word that stands in for a noun, like “he”, “she”, “it”, “we” or “you”. In plain words. Pronouns save us from repeating a name over and over. Instead of saying “Mary took Mary’s coat because Mary was cold”, we say “Mary took her coat because she was cold.” Common pronouns are I, me, my, you, your, he, him, his, she, her, it, we, us, our, they, them, their, and also who, whom, this and that. A pronoun always points to someone or something already named or clear from the setting (see Antecedent ). An everyday example. “Grandpa lost his glasses, so we helped him find them .” His, we, him and them are all pronouns. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Small pronouns can carry great comfort. “My shepherd” is far warmer than “a shepherd”. When you meet “us”, “we” or “our”, ask who is included. When you meet “he” or “him”, make sure you know who is meant before you build on the verse. Some of the sweetest words in Scripture are the little ones: me and for me . Psalm 23:1 The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. The pronoun “my” turns a general truth into a personal confession. David is not only saying the LORD is a shepherd, but that he is David’s own shepherd. Galatians 2:20 who loved me and gave himself for me. Paul uses “me” twice. Christ’s love is not only for people in general; it reaches the individual believer by name. Pronouns turn doctrine into personal trust: “my shepherd”, “loved me”.

Antecedent The antecedent is the person or thing that a pronoun points back to. In plain words. A pronoun like “he” or “it” is a pointer (see Pronoun ). The antecedent is whatever it points back to. The word just means “the one that goes before”. Usually the antecedent comes earlier in the sentence or in the sentence before. To find it, ask: “Who is he ? What is it ?” An everyday example. “The dog chased the cat until it was tired.” Was the dog tired, or the cat? That little puzzle is exactly the question of the antecedent. Most of the time the meaning is clear; sometimes it takes a second look. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Getting the antecedent right is one of the simplest and most useful habits in Bible reading. In long sentences, such as Paul’s, a “who”, “which” or “this” may point back several lines. Greek helps a little, because its pronouns often show whether they are masculine, feminine or neuter, and they must match what they point to. Sometimes good scholars still disagree about an antecedent, so hold such points humbly and let the wider passage decide. Ephesians 2:8 For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, What does “this” point back to? In Greek “this” is neuter, while “grace” and “faith” are feminine, so many Reformed readers take it to mean the whole thing: being saved by grace through faith. Either way, nothing in our salvation is our own doing. Ephesians 1:14 who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, “Who” points back to “the promised Holy Spirit” at the end of verse 13. The Spirit himself is God’s pledge that the full inheritance will come. When a pronoun puzzles you, find its antecedent first; the meaning usually opens up.

Verb A verb is a doing or being word: it tells you what someone does, what happens, or what something is. In plain words. Every full sentence needs a verb. Most verbs are action words: run, speak, create, save, love. Some verbs describe a state rather than an action: is, was, remain, seem. Verbs also tell you when something happens (past, present or future), and whether someone does the action or has it done to them. Those ideas have their own cards in the section on verbs. An everyday example. “The children laughed .” “Dinner is ready.” “Grandma will bake a cake.” Each bold word or word group is the verb. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The verbs of a passage often tell the story of the gospel. Look at who is doing them. Very often in Scripture the great verbs belong to God: he creates, chooses, calls, justifies, gives. Our verbs (believe, repent, obey) follow his and respond to them. Reading with an eye on the verbs, and on who their doer is, keeps grace at the centre. Genesis 1:1 In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. The verb is “created”, and its doer is God. The Bible opens with God acting, before anything else exists. John 11:35 Jesus wept. A whole sentence made of a name and a verb. The verb “wept” shows the true humanity and tender heart of the Son of God. Ask of every verse: what is being done, and who is doing it?

Adjective An adjective is a describing word: it tells you more about a noun. In plain words. An adjective answers questions like “What kind?”, “Which one?” or “How many?” about a person or thing (see Noun ). Big, small, red, kind, holy, good, eternal and three are all adjectives. An adjective usually sits just before its noun (“a good shepherd”) or after a verb like “is” (“the shepherd is good ”). An everyday example. “We stayed in a small , cosy cottage with a green door.” The bold words describe the cottage and the door. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Adjectives tell us what something is like, and in the Bible they often describe God and his gifts. A gift is not just life, but eternal life; not just a shepherd, but the good shepherd. When an adjective is repeated, Hebrew is giving it the strongest possible emphasis. Pay attention to adjectives: they often hold the very point the writer wants you to feel. John 10:11 I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. The adjective “good” sets Jesus apart from hired hands and false shepherds. Then the verse shows what his goodness looks like: he lays down his life. Isaiah 6:3 Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; Hebrew had no simple word for “most”, so it repeats the adjective. Saying it three times means holy beyond all comparison. Adjectives tell you what God and his gifts are like; repeated ones are shouting.

Adverb An adverb tells you how, when, where or how much something happens. In plain words. An adverb usually adds detail to a verb (see Verb ). It answers questions like “How?” (quickly, gladly, bitterly), “When?” (now, today, always, once), “Where?” (here, there, above) or “How much?” (very, greatly). Many English adverbs end in “-ly”, but not all do: “now”, “always” and “once” are adverbs too. An everyday example. “She sang softly .” (How?) “We leave tomorrow .” (When?) “Come here .” (Where?) Why it matters when you read the Bible. Adverbs are small, but they can carry big doctrines. “Now” can mark the change the gospel has made. “Once” can mark that Christ’s sacrifice needs no repeating. “Always” can turn a promise into lasting comfort. When you see an adverb, ask what difference it makes to the sentence, and what the verse would lose without it. Romans 8:1 There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. The adverb “now” tells you when: not only one day at the judgment, but already, today, for those in Christ. 1 Peter 3:18 For Christ also suffered once for sins, The adverb “once” stresses that his suffering for sins was a single, complete act. Hebrews makes the same point: it never needs to be repeated. Luke 22:62 And he went out and wept bitterly. “Bitterly” tells us how Peter wept after denying Jesus: real sorrow for sin, which the risen Lord later met with restoring grace. Adverbs like “now”, “once” and “always” often hold the comfort of a verse.

Article An article is one of the little words “the”, “a” or “an” that come before a noun. In plain words. English has two kinds of article. “The” points to a particular one that you know about. “A” or “an” means one of many, not a particular one. Greek is different: it has a word for “the”, but no word for “a” at all. So when Greek has no “the”, translators must decide from the context whether English needs “a”, “the”, or no article at all. An everyday example. “I saw a dog” (any dog). “I saw the dog” (the one we were talking about). One small word changes the meaning. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The Greek “the” can point to someone well known (“the Christ”). But its absence does not mean “a”. In John 1:1 the last clause in Greek reads, word for word, “God was the Word”. Some groups translate this “the Word was a god”. That is wrong. In the same chapter John writes “a man sent from God” (1:6) and “No one has ever seen God” (1:18) with no article before “God”, and nobody translates those “a god”. Greek grammar leaves out the article here because “God” describes what the Word is, while “the Word” is the subject. John is saying the Word is truly God, and yet is distinct from the Father he was “with”. John 1:1 and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. “With God” has the article in Greek (with the God, meaning the Father); “was God” does not. The Word is fully God in nature, yet a distinct person who is with the Father. John 14:6 I am the way, and the truth, and the life. Jesus does not say he is a way among many. The article points to him as the one and only way to the Father. Small words matter: “the way” is not “a way”, and missing articles in Greek do not mean “a”.

Preposition A preposition is a small word that shows how one thing relates to another, such as “in”, “on”, “with”, “from”, “to” or “through”. In plain words. Prepositions are linking words of place, time and relationship. They answer questions like “Where?” (in the house, under the table), “When?” (before dawn, after supper) and “How or why?” (by faith, for you, with love). A preposition never stands alone: it always leads into a noun or pronoun, as in “to him ” or “through faith ”. An everyday example. “The keys are on the table, beside the lamp.” “We walked through the park after lunch.” Why it matters when you read the Bible. In the Bible, prepositions often describe how God, Christ and believers relate to each other. Change the preposition and you change the doctrine: salvation is by grace and through faith, not because of works. Greek prepositions can have more than one meaning, so careful readers look at the context rather than assuming one fixed sense. The next card looks at the prepositions at the heart of the gospel. Romans 11:36 For from him and through him and to him are all things. Three prepositions say it all: everything comes from God, holds together through God, and exists for God. So Paul ends: To him be glory forever. Ephesians 2:8 For by grace you have been saved through faith. Grace is the source; faith is the channel. Faith is not the reason we are saved, but the empty hand that receives the gift. Prepositions often carry the logic of a doctrine; read them slowly.

Prepositions that carry the gospel Four little words, “in”, “through”, “for” and “with”, sum up how believers are joined to Christ and saved by him. In plain words. Some short prepositions (see Preposition ) are used again and again in the New Testament to describe what Christ has done for us. In Christ means united to him, belonging to him, as a branch is in a vine. Through Christ means by his work, as the one who brings us to God. For us (or “on behalf of us”) means for our benefit and in our place. With Christ means sharing in what happened to him: his death, his rising, his life. An everyday example. “I am in the family.” “The parcel came through the post.” “He paid for me.” “She came home with me.” Each word tells a different kind of relationship. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Paul can sum up the Christian life in these words. Note one point of care: the Greek word usually behind “for” ( hyper ) means “on behalf of”. On its own it does not prove that Christ took our place. But in passages like 2 Corinthians 5:21 and 1 Peter 3:18, the context makes clear that he stood where we should have stood. These words are not dry grammar; they describe the believer’s whole standing before God. Romans 8:1 There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Freedom from condemnation belongs to those “in Christ Jesus”, joined to him by faith. Romans 5:1 we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Peace comes “through” Christ: he is the one by whom we are brought to God. Romans 5:8 but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. “For us” means on our behalf. Christ’s death was for people who were still sinners, not for people who had cleaned themselves up. In him, through him, for us, with him: four prepositions that carry the whole gospel.

Conjunction A conjunction is a joining word, like “and”, “but”, “or”, “for”, “because” or “therefore”. In plain words. Conjunctions join words, phrases or whole sentences together, and they show how the ideas relate. “And” adds. “But” turns or contrasts. “Or” gives a choice. “For” and “because” give a reason. “So” and “therefore” draw a conclusion. They are like the hinges of a door: small, but everything swings on them. An everyday example. “I was tired, but I kept walking.” “It rained, so we stayed in.” “Take your coat, because it is cold.” Why it matters when you read the Bible. Paul’s letters are full of reasoning, and conjunctions show you how the argument moves. A well-known saying is: when you see “therefore”, ask what it is there for. Often it points back to everything God has done before it tells you what to do. “But” can mark a dramatic turn, from our ruin to God’s rescue. Learning to notice these words is one of the best ways to follow a passage’s train of thought (see also the cards on Joining Ideas ). Ephesians 2:4 But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, After three verses describing us as dead in sin, the single word “But” turns everything. Our hopelessness is met by God’s mercy. Romans 12:1 I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, “Therefore” points back to eleven chapters of God’s mercy. The call to holy living rests on grace already given, not the other way round. “But” and “therefore” are hinges: watch for them and you will follow the argument.

Interjection An interjection is a cry or exclamation like “Oh!”, “Look!” or “Alas!” that expresses feeling or calls for attention. In plain words. An interjection is a word thrown into speech to show strong feeling or to grab attention. It usually stands a little apart from the rest of the sentence, often with an exclamation mark. Bible English has some special ones. “Behold” means “Look!” or “Pay attention!”. “O” is used when speaking to someone with deep feeling (see Vocative ). “Oh” expresses wonder or longing. “Woe” expresses grief or warning. An everyday example. “ Oh , what a lovely surprise!” “ Look , there is a rainbow!” “ Ouch , that hurt!” Why it matters when you read the Bible. Interjections tell you how a verse should be felt, not only what it says. When the Bible says “Behold”, it is tapping you on the shoulder: stop and look carefully at what comes next. When Paul cries “Oh, the depth”, he has run out of argument and broken into worship. Good reading lets those words move the heart as well as inform the mind. John 1:29 Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! “Behold” calls everyone to look at Jesus. The whole Old Testament sacrifice system was pointing to this one person. Romans 11:33 Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! After explaining God’s saving plan, Paul bursts into praise. Sound doctrine should end in worship. Psalm 8:1 O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth! “O” marks warm, wondering address to God. The psalm is spoken to him, not only about him. “Behold” means stop and look; “Oh” means the writer is overwhelmed.

Sentence A sentence is a group of words that makes a complete thought. In plain words. A sentence makes sense on its own. In English it starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark. Every full sentence has someone or something it is about (see Subject ) and something said about it, which always includes a verb (see Verb ). Sentences can be very short or very long. Note that the verse numbers in our Bibles were added much later; a sentence can run across several verses, and a verse can hold several sentences. An everyday example. “Dogs bark.” is a complete sentence. “When the dogs bark” is not: it leaves you waiting for more. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Always read a verse as part of its whole sentence. Many verses begin halfway through a sentence, and their meaning depends on what came before. In Greek, Ephesians 1:3 to 1:14 is one single, long sentence of praise, piling blessing upon blessing. At the other end, “Jesus wept” is the shortest verse in most English Bibles, and a complete sentence. Finding where a sentence starts and ends is the first step to reading it rightly. Ephesians 1:3 Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, Notice the comma at the end. In Greek this sentence keeps going until verse 14, as if Paul cannot stop praising God for his blessings in Christ. John 11:35 Jesus wept. Two words, one complete sentence: someone (Jesus) and something said about him (wept). Read whole sentences, not just verses: the verse numbers are later helps, not part of the text.

Subject The subject is the person or thing a sentence is about, usually the one doing the action. In plain words. To find the subject, find the verb (the doing word) and ask: “Who or what is doing this?” The answer is the subject. In “The boy kicked the ball”, who kicked? The boy. So “the boy” is the subject. With a verb like “is”, the subject is the one being described: in “The soup is hot”, the subject is “the soup”. An everyday example. “ My sister baked a cake.” Who baked? My sister: that is the subject. “ The bus was late.” What was late? The bus. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Asking “Who is the subject?” is one of the most important questions in Bible reading, because it shows who is doing the saving. Again and again the subject of the great verbs of salvation is God, not us. That does not make our response unimportant, but it puts it in its place: we act because he has acted first. When you are unsure what a verse means, find the verb and then find its subject. 1 John 4:10 In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son John swaps the subject on purpose. Love is not first “we loved God”, but “he loved us”. God is the subject of the love that saves. Romans 5:8 but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Who shows love? God. Who died? Christ. The subjects of this verse are God and his Son; we are only the ones it is done for. Find the verb, then ask who is doing it: very often the answer is God.

Object The object is the person or thing that receives the action of the verb. In plain words. If the subject is the one doing the action (see Subject ), the object is the one the action is done to. To find it, take the verb and ask: “Whom?” or “What?” In “The boy kicked the ball”, kicked what? The ball. So “the ball” is the object. Some sentences also have a second kind of object, the one who receives something: in “She gave him a book”, the book is what she gave, and “him” is the one who received it. An everyday example. “Dad washed the car .” Washed what? The car. “The teacher praised us .” Praised whom? Us. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Spotting the object helps you see who is acted upon. In the gospel we are very often the object: God chose us , loved us , saved us . That is humbling, because we contribute nothing, and comforting, because it rests on him. In Greek the object is usually shown by the ending of the word rather than by word order, which is why translators work carefully to show who did what to whom. 1 John 4:10 but that he loved us and sent his Son “Us” is the object of “loved”, and “his Son” is the object of “sent”. We receive God’s love; we do not start it. Ephesians 1:4 even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, God is the subject, “us” is the object. Our election is something done to us, by God, before we existed. In the verbs of salvation we are usually the object: grace is something done to us.

Clause A clause is a group of words with its own subject and verb, a building block of a sentence. In plain words. A clause is like a mini-sentence inside a sentence. It has a subject (who or what) and a verb (what they do or are). A simple sentence has one clause: “Jesus wept.” Longer sentences join several clauses together, often with linking words like “and”, “but”, “because”, “when” or “if” (see Conjunction ). Some clauses could stand alone; others depend on another clause (see Main clause and subordinate clause ). An everyday example. “ I made tea and you made toast .” Two clauses, each with a subject and a verb, joined by “and”. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Breaking a long Bible sentence into its clauses is a simple way to understand it. Write each clause on its own line, and look at how they connect. You will often find that one clause gives a reason, another a time, another a purpose. Paul’s long sentences become clear once you see their clauses, and you start to follow his thinking from step to step. Romans 5:8 but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Three clauses: God shows his love; we were still sinners; Christ died for us. The middle one sets the time: Christ died while we were still sinners, not after we had improved. John 15:5 I am the vine; you are the branches. Two short clauses, each with its own subject and verb, side by side. The picture is complete only when you hold them together. Split a long sentence into its clauses and its logic usually becomes plain.

Main clause and subordinate clause A main clause can stand on its own; a subordinate clause leans on it and adds information like when, why, or on what condition. In plain words. A sentence is often built from a main clause plus one or more helper clauses (see Clause ). The main clause carries the central statement and makes sense by itself. A subordinate clause cannot stand alone; it usually begins with a word like “because”, “since”, “when”, “if”, “although”, “so that” or “who”. It tells you why, when, under what condition, for what purpose, or which person. An everyday example. “ We stayed indoors because it was raining.” The main clause is “We stayed indoors”. “Because it was raining” tells us why, but it cannot stand on its own. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Finding the main clause shows you the main point; the subordinate clauses show the reasons and conditions around it. This often keeps the order of salvation clear. For example, our peace with God is the main statement, and being justified by faith is the reason it rests on. If you mix them up, you can easily turn a result into a cause. Careful readers ask: what is the main statement here, and what is supporting it? Romans 5:1 Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Main clause: “we have peace with God”. Subordinate clause: “since we have been justified by faith”. Peace is the result; justification is its ground. 1 John 1:9 If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins “If we confess our sins” is the condition; the main clause tells you what God will be. The promise rests on God’s faithfulness, not on the quality of our confession. Find the main clause for the main point; the subordinate clauses tell you why, when and how.

Phrase A phrase is a small group of words that belong together but do not have their own subject and verb. In plain words. A phrase works like a single unit inside a sentence. Unlike a clause (see Clause ), it does not have its own subject and verb. Examples are “in the morning”, “the love of God”, “by faith” and “in Christ Jesus”. Phrases often add detail about where, when, how or whose. An everyday example. “We walked along the river after breakfast .” Each bold group is a phrase, telling where and when. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Some of the most important ideas in the Bible are held in short phrases. “In Christ” occurs again and again in Paul’s letters. “The righteousness of God” and “the love of God” are phrases that need careful thought: is it God’s own love, or our love for God? Usually the context tells you, and Bible teachers often discuss such phrases. When a phrase keeps coming back, it is worth tracing it through a letter. Romans 8:39 nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Two phrases close the verse: “the love of God” and “in Christ Jesus our Lord”. Here it clearly means God’s love for us, and it is found in Christ. Ephesians 1:3 who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, Three phrases: “in Christ”, “with every spiritual blessing”, “in the heavenly places”. Each adds to the picture of what God has given. Watch for phrases that keep returning, like “in Christ”: they are often the heart of a letter.

Statement, question and command Sentences come in different kinds: a statement tells, a question asks, and a command tells someone to do something. In plain words. Most sentences are one of three kinds. A statement tells you something is so: “The door is open.” A question asks something: “Is the door open?” A command tells someone to do something: “Open the door.” There is also the exclamation, which expresses strong feeling: “What a door!” Each kind of sentence does a different job. An everyday example. “It is cold.” (statement) “Are you cold?” (question) “Shut the window!” (command) Why it matters when you read the Bible. The Bible uses all of these, and it matters which you are reading. A statement of what God has done is a truth to believe. A command is a call to obey. In Paul’s letters, statements about what God has done usually come before the commands about how to live. Grace comes first, and obedience follows from it. Keeping that order helps us avoid trying to earn what God has already given. Matthew 11:28 Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. A command (“Come to me”) joined to a promise (“I will give you rest”). The command is really a warm invitation. Colossians 3:1 If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, A statement of fact about believers (“you have been raised with Christ”) is followed by a command (“seek”). The command grows out of what is already true. Statements tell you what God has done; commands tell you how to live in response.

Rhetorical question A rhetorical question is a question asked not to get an answer, but to make a point. In plain words. Sometimes we ask a question when the answer is already obvious. We are not really asking; we are making a point in a lively way. That is a rhetorical question. It invites the listener to answer in their own mind, and so to agree. An everyday example. A mother says, “How many times have I told you to wipe your feet?” She does not want a number. She means: “I have told you many times!” Why it matters when you read the Bible. The Bible often teaches through rhetorical questions, especially Paul. They draw us in and make us think the answer for ourselves. They can also answer an objection: Paul raises a wrong idea as a question, then rejects it firmly. When you meet such a question, pause and answer it in your heart; the answer is usually a great comfort or a strong warning. Romans 8:31 If God is for us, who can be against us? Paul does not expect a list of enemies. The point is: no one can succeed against those whom God is for. Romans 8:32 He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? The obvious answer is: of course he will. If God gave the greatest gift, he will not hold back lesser ones. Romans 6:1 Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? Paul raises a wrong conclusion as a question, then answers it in verse 2: By no means! Answer a rhetorical question in your own heart: that is what it is for.

Word order and emphasis Moving a word to the front of a sentence can make it stand out. In plain words. In English, word order is fairly fixed: usually the subject, then the verb, then the object (see Subject and Object ). Greek and Hebrew are freer, because the endings of words show who does what. That freedom lets writers put a word first, or in an unusual place, to give it extra weight. English translations cannot always copy that order, so the emphasis can be lost in translation. An everyday example. Compare “I will never forget that day” with “ That day I will never forget.” Putting “that day” first makes it stand out. Why it matters when you read the Bible. A word placed first in Greek is often, though not always, being stressed. Sometimes the order is just natural style, so do not build too much on it alone. But where commentators point out emphatic word order, it can add colour. In Ephesians 2:8 the Greek begins with “by grace”, putting it in the spotlight. In Galatians 2:20 Paul’s sentence begins with “Christ”, word for word “With Christ I have been crucified”. Ephesians 2:8 For by grace you have been saved through faith. Here English keeps the Greek order: “by grace” comes first, putting God’s free favour in the spotlight. Galatians 2:20 I have been crucified with Christ. In Greek, “Christ” is the first word of the sentence. Paul’s life now begins and ends with his union with Christ. Word order can add emphasis in Greek, but it is a hint, not a proof.

Apposition Apposition is when a second name or description is placed right next to the first to explain it. In plain words. Sometimes a writer names a person or thing, then immediately adds another name for the same person or thing, usually set off by commas. The second part does not add a new person; it explains or renames the first. That is apposition. The word means “placed beside”. An everyday example. “My neighbour, a retired nurse , helped me.” The neighbour and the retired nurse are the same person. “London, the capital , was busy.” Why it matters when you read the Bible. Apposition helps you see how the Bible defines its own words. When Paul places two phrases side by side, he is often telling you what the first means. It also shows the richness of Christ’s names: one title after another, each describing the same Lord. Noticing it keeps you from thinking a verse speaks of two different things when it is speaking of one. Ephesians 1:7 In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, “The forgiveness of our trespasses” is in apposition to “redemption”. Paul explains that being redeemed means, at its heart, being forgiven. Matthew 16:16 You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. “The Son of the living God” stands beside “the Christ” to explain who the promised Messiah truly is. When two descriptions sit side by side, the second often explains the first.

Singular and plural Singular means one; plural means more than one. In plain words. A singular word speaks of one person or thing: “a child”, “he”, “I”. A plural word speaks of more than one: “children”, “they”, “we”. Old English had a separate word for “you” when speaking to one person (“thou”, “thee”), but modern English uses “you” for both. Greek and Hebrew, like old English, have different forms for “you” singular and “you” plural, so readers of the original can always tell. An everyday example. “Are you coming?” could be asked of one friend or of a whole family. In some places people say “you all” or “you guys” to make the plural clear. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Many “you”s in the New Testament letters are plural: they speak to the whole church together. That changes how we read some verses. In 1 Corinthians 3:16 “you” is plural: the church together is God’s temple. In 1 Corinthians 6:19 Paul applies a similar picture to each believer’s body. Both are true, but they are different verses with different points. When a commentary notes that “you” is plural, it is pointing you to the life of God’s people together. 1 Corinthians 3:16 Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? Every “you” here is plural in Greek. The church as a community is the temple where the Spirit dwells. Luke 22:31 Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, Here “you” is plural: Satan wanted to sift all the disciples. Luke 22:32 but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. Now “you” is singular: Jesus prayed for Peter personally. Greek shows both the danger to all and the care for one. A plural “you” often means the church together, not only the individual reader.

Vocative The vocative is the form used when you speak directly to someone, calling them by name. In plain words. When we call someone by name or title, we are speaking directly to them: “John, come here!” or “Lord, help me.” That calling-word is the vocative. In English it is usually set off by commas. Greek often has a special ending for it. Words like “O” before a name are a sign of direct address (see Interjection ). An everyday example. “ Mum , where are my shoes?” “Thank you, doctor .” The bold words address the person spoken to. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Vocatives show how people speak to God, and how he speaks to them. Jesus addressed God as “Abba, Father”, using the warm Aramaic word a child used for his father, together with the Greek word for Father. Through the Spirit of adoption, believers share that same right to call God Father (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). Vocatives also show God’s tenderness: Jesus calls “Simon, Simon” before warning and comforting him. Mark 14:36 Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. In Gethsemane Jesus speaks to God with closest intimacy. “Abba” is not baby talk, but it is a word of trust from a son to his father. Romans 8:15 but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, What follows in this verse is the vocative “Abba! Father!”. The Spirit lets adopted children speak to God the way the Son does. Psalm 103:1 Bless the LORD, O my soul, David uses a vocative to speak to his own soul, stirring himself up to praise. The vocative shows the relationship: believers may call God “Abba, Father”.

Tense Tense is the part of a verb that tells you when something happens, and sometimes how it happens. In plain words. A verb is a doing word, like run , love or save (see Verb ). The tense of a verb is the little change in its form that shows when the action happens: in the past, now, or later. In English we often change the ending ( walk , walked ) or add a helping word ( will walk , have walked ). In Greek, tense also tells you what kind of action it is: something going on, something simply done, or something finished with lasting results. Do not worry if this feels new. You use tenses every day without thinking about them. An everyday example. “I walked to the shop.” (past) “I am walking to the shop.” (now, going on) “I will walk to the shop.” (later) Same verb, three different times, just by changing its form. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Tense helps you see whether the Bible is describing something God has already done, something he is doing now, or something he promises to do. Paul in Galatians 2:20 puts a finished past (“I have been crucified with Christ”) beside an ongoing present (“Christ who lives in me”). Notice how the past work of Christ becomes the ground of daily life now. Good English translations carry most of this over, so you can usually see it just by reading carefully. Galatians 2:20 I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. “Have been crucified” looks back to something done, with lasting effect. “Lives” is present: Christ goes on living in the believer today. Philippians 1:6 he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ. Two tenses side by side: “began” (past) and “will bring” (future). What God started, he will surely finish. Noticing when an action happens helps you tell God’s finished work from his ongoing work and his sure promises.

Past, present and future Past means it already happened, present means it is happening now, and future means it is still to come. In plain words. These are the three basic times a verb can point to. The past is behind us: it already happened. The present is now: it is happening as we speak. The future is ahead: it has not happened yet but is expected. English shows these with endings and small helping words such as did , is and will . That is really all there is to it. An everyday example. “Yesterday I baked bread.” (past) “Today I am eating it.” (present) “Tomorrow I will share it.” (future) Why it matters when you read the Bible. The Bible often places all three times together to show that God is faithful across them all. Our salvation has a past (Christ died and rose for us), a present (he lives and prays for us now) and a future (he will come again). When you notice which time a verse is speaking about, you avoid mixing up what is already true with what is still promised. For example, a believer has already been forgiven, is being changed now, and will one day be made perfect. Hebrews 13:8 Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. Past (“yesterday”), present (“today”) and future (“forever”) in one line. Christ does not change in any of them. Revelation 1:8 who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty. God is described with present (“is”), past (“was”) and future (“is to come”). He is Lord over every time. God is Lord of past, present and future, so every promise rests on the same unchanging God.

Present continuous The present continuous describes an action that keeps going on, not just one that happens once. In plain words. Some verbs describe a single moment: he jumped . Others describe something that carries on: he keeps jumping , he is jumping . In English we show ongoing action with is or are plus an -ing word, or with words like keeps on . Greek often shows the same idea with its present tense, which very often (though not always) pictures an action as going on. An everyday example. “She smokes ” does not mean she lit one cigarette once. It means it is her habit. Compare “she is smoking right now” (going on at this moment) with “she smoked once at a party” (a single event). Why it matters when you read the Bible. This matters a great deal in 1 John. Read quickly, 1 John 3:6 and 3:9 could seem to say that a true Christian never sins at all, which would crush any honest believer. But John has already said that we do sin and must confess it (1 John 1:9; 2:1). His present tense verbs describe a settled habit, a way of life. The ESV shows this with “keeps on sinning” and “makes a practice of sinning”. A Christian still stumbles, but no longer lives at peace with sin as a pattern, because God’s new life is at work within. 1 John 3:6 No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him. “Keeps on sinning” translates a Greek present that describes a continuing pattern, not every single slip. 1 John 3:9 No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God’s seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God. “Makes a practice of” shows the ongoing sense. The reason is God’s work: the believer “has been born of God”. 1 Corinthians 1:18 but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. “Are being saved” is ongoing. Salvation is something God is working out in us day by day. Seeing ongoing action keeps us from both despair (“I still sin, so I am lost”) and carelessness (“sin does not matter”).

Perfect tense The perfect tense describes something that was done in the past and whose results still last today. In plain words. The perfect tense joins two ideas: an action that is complete, and a result that remains. In English we usually show it with has or have : I have written , it is finished . Greek has a special form for this, and New Testament writers often chose it carefully. Think of it as “done, and it stays done”. An everyday example. “I have locked the door.” The locking happened a moment ago, but the point is that the door is still locked now. “The cake is baked ” means the baking is over and you now have a cake. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Some of the most comforting words in Scripture use the perfect. When Jesus cried “It is finished”, he used a single Greek word in the perfect: the work of paying for sin was done, and it stands done for ever. When he answered Satan with “It is written”, he meant: God wrote it, and it still stands as his word today. And when Paul says “by grace you have been saved”, he means salvation is not a fragile thing that may come undone; it was accomplished and it remains. A believer can rest on that. John 19:30 he said, “It is finished,” One Greek word in the perfect tense: the work is complete and its result lasts. Nothing needs to be added to Christ’s sacrifice. Matthew 4:4 It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.’ “It is written” is perfect: God’s word was written and still stands with full authority. Ephesians 2:8 For by grace you have been saved through faith. “Have been saved” is perfect: a finished act of God with a lasting result. Your salvation stands secure. The perfect tense lets you rest in what God has done and what therefore remains true.

Aorist The aorist is a Greek verb form that simply states that something happened, without describing how long it took. In plain words. The aorist (say it “AIR-ist”) is the most common past form in Greek. It presents an action as a whole, like a snapshot, without saying whether it was long, short, repeated or once only. It is the plain, ordinary way to say “he did it”. English usually translates it as a simple past: he went , she loved . Some preachers say the aorist means “once for all”. That is not right. The aorist by itself only states that the action happened. If an action was once for all, the words around it must show that. An everyday example. “I lived in Scotland.” That tells you it happened, but not whether it was for a week or forty years. You need more words to know. The aorist works in the same simple way. Why it matters when you read the Bible. This keeps us honest. When the Bible teaches that Christ died once for all, it says so with a separate word meaning “once for all” (Greek ephapax ), as in Romans 6:10 and Hebrews 10:10. That doctrine is gloriously true, but it rests on those words, not on the aorist alone. In fact “all have sinned” in Romans 3:23 is also an aorist, and that is certainly not one single sin. So be careful when a sermon builds a big point on the aorist alone; look at the whole sentence. Romans 6:10 For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, “Once for all” is a separate Greek word. It, not the aorist verb, tells us Christ’s death will never be repeated. Romans 3:23 for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, “Have sinned” is an aorist, yet it covers a whole lifetime of sins by all people. The aorist does not mean a single act. Hebrews 10:10 And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. Again the phrase “once for all” carries the meaning. Christ’s one offering is enough for ever. Do not make the aorist say more than it says; let the whole sentence speak.

Imperfect The imperfect describes something that was going on in the past, like a film rather than a photograph. In plain words. The imperfect is a Greek past tense that pictures an action as ongoing, repeated or in progress at some time in the past. Where the aorist is a snapshot, the imperfect is like a moving picture. English often translates it with was or were plus an -ing word ( he was teaching ), or with words like used to or kept . The name does not mean faulty. It simply means “not completed” at that moment. An everyday example. “When the phone rang, I was cooking supper.” The cooking was going on when something else happened. Or: “As a boy I used to walk to school.” That was a habit in the past. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The imperfect can open a window onto scenes in the Gospels and Acts. It shows Jesus teaching in the synagogue as an ongoing activity, and the first church continuing in the apostles’ teaching, not just attending once. In John 1:1 the verb “was” describes the Word as simply existing in the beginning, with no point when he began, while John 1:14 uses a different verb for when he “became” flesh. That contrast supports what Christians confess: the Son is eternal, and in time he took on our nature. Mark 1:21 on the Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching. “Entered” is a simple past; “was teaching” pictures the teaching as going on. John 1:1 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. “Was” is an imperfect of being: when the beginning began, the Word already was. He did not come into being. Acts 2:42 And they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers. The Greek describes an ongoing devotion. The early believers kept on doing these things. The imperfect shows that some things in Scripture were ongoing patterns, not one-off moments.

Future The future tense tells you about something that has not happened yet but will happen. In plain words. The future tense points ahead. In English we form it with will or shall : I will go , they shall see . In Greek the verb itself changes its form. When a person speaks in the future, he is predicting, planning or promising. When God speaks in the future, it is a promise as sure as if it were already done. An everyday example. “I will meet you at the station at six.” That is a promise about later. Whether it comes true depends on whether the speaker is reliable. Why it matters when you read the Bible. God is perfectly reliable, so his future tenses are solid ground. Jesus says “I will come again”, and “whoever comes to me I will never cast out”. Paul says God “will bring it to completion”. These are not hopeful wishes but promises from one who cannot lie. Notice also that the Bible sometimes uses the future for commands, as in “You shall not murder”. The setting tells you whether a future verb is a promise, a prediction or a command. John 14:3 I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. Two future promises: Christ “will come” and “will take” us. Our hope rests on his word. John 6:37 All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out. The futures are certain: the Father’s people “will come”, and Christ “will never cast out” anyone who comes. When God speaks in the future tense, believers can treat it as settled.

Active voice In the active voice, the person or thing doing the action is the subject of the sentence. In plain words. Every sentence has someone or something it is mainly about, called the subject (see Subject ). When the subject is the one doing the action, the verb is in the active voice. “Voice” is just the grammar word for who is doing what. Most sentences you speak are active. The doer comes first and then the deed. An everyday example. “ The dog bit the postman.” The dog is the subject, and the dog did the biting. That is active. (Compare the passive: “The postman was bitten by the dog.”) Why it matters when you read the Bible. Active verbs put the spotlight on the doer. In the gospel the great doer is God. “God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son.” “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.” These active verbs make clear who took the initiative in our salvation: not us, but God in Christ. When you read, it is a good habit to ask of each main verb: who is doing this? Often the answer is the heart of the verse. John 3:16 For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, God is the subject and does the loving and the giving. Salvation begins with God’s action. Ephesians 5:25 as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, Christ is the doer of both verbs. His active love is the pattern for a husband’s love. Asking “who is doing this?” often brings you straight to the heart of a verse.

Passive voice A passive verb tells you what was done to someone, not what they did. In plain words. In the passive voice the subject of the sentence (see Subject ) is not the doer but the one something happens to. English shows it with a form of be plus a word like saved , given or forgiven : was saved , are forgiven . Sometimes the doer is named with “by”; sometimes the doer is left unnamed. An everyday example. “The window was broken .” The window did nothing; something happened to it. “The window was broken by the ball ” adds who or what did it. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Passive verbs are everywhere in the Bible’s teaching about salvation, and they are deeply humbling and comforting. We “are justified”, we “were sealed”, our sins “are forgiven”. In each case we are the ones receiving, and God is the one acting. We do not justify ourselves or seal ourselves. A passive verb quietly preaches grace: it tells you that what saves you is something done to you and for you, not something you achieved. Romans 3:24 and are justified by his grace as a gift, “Are justified” is passive. We receive God’s verdict; we do not earn it. Ephesians 1:13 were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, “Were sealed” is passive. God himself places his mark of ownership on believers. 1 Corinthians 6:11 But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God. Three verbs describing what was done for believers. The end of the verse names the doers: the Lord Jesus Christ and the Spirit. A passive verb in a salvation verse is a small sermon on grace.

Divine passive A divine passive is a passive verb where God is the hidden doer, even though he is not named. In plain words. Sometimes the Bible uses a passive verb (see Passive voice ) and does not say who does the action. Very often the hidden doer is God. Scholars call this the “divine passive”. Jewish speakers sometimes spoke this way out of reverence for God’s name, and it was a natural way to speak of what only God can do. You discover the hidden doer by asking: “Who could do this?” An everyday example. If a child is told, “Your bike has been mended ,” and the child knows that only Dad mends bikes in that house, the child knows who did it without being told. Why it matters when you read the Bible. In the Beatitudes Jesus says those who mourn “shall be comforted”. Comforted by whom? By God himself. In “Ask, and it will be given to you”, God is the giver. When Jesus told the paralysed man, “your sins are forgiven”, the hearers rightly realised that only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7), and so his words were a claim to divine authority. A little caution: not every passive hides God. Let the setting guide you. But where it does, the verse becomes a personal promise from God. Matthew 5:4 Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. “Shall be comforted” leaves the doer unnamed. God is the one who comforts. Matthew 7:7 Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. “Will be given” and “will be opened” are divine passives. God is the one who gives and opens. Mark 2:5 he said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” The passive hides the doer, but only God forgives sins. Jesus speaks with God’s own authority. Ask “who could do this?”, and many passive verses turn into personal promises from God.

Middle voice The middle voice is a Greek verb form where the subject acts with a special interest in itself or for its own sake. In plain words. English has two voices: active (I wash the car) and passive (the car is washed). Greek has a third, called the middle , because it sits between the two. In the middle voice the doer is also closely involved in the result: doing something to yourself, for yourself, or with your own personal share in it. English has no special form for this, so translators use words like yourself , or simply choose a good verb. Some Greek verbs also look middle but simply mean an ordinary active idea, so the middle does not always carry a special meaning. An everyday example. “I washed myself ” or “I got myself a coffee.” The person both does the action and is personally touched by it. That is the feel of the Greek middle. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The middle voice can add a quiet personal colour. In Ephesians 6:11 Paul tells believers to “put on” the armour of God, using a middle form: clothe yourselves with it. In Acts 22:16 Ananias tells Paul to “wash away your sins”, again a middle form, which some take as “have your sins washed away” as Paul calls on the Lord’s name. That reading fits the rest of Scripture, where only God cleanses. Because the middle is subtle and scholars debate some cases, it is wise not to build doctrine on it alone. Ephesians 6:11 Put on the whole armor of God, “Put on” is middle: clothe yourselves. The armour is God’s, but each believer is personally to wear it. Acts 22:16 Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name. “Wash away” is middle. The cleansing comes as Paul calls on the Lord, who alone washes sin away. The middle voice adds personal colour, but it is too subtle to carry a doctrine by itself.

Mood Mood is the form of a verb that shows whether you are stating a fact, giving a command, or talking about a possibility or wish. In plain words. Verbs do not only show time (see Tense ). They also show the speaker’s attitude to the action. That is called the mood. Is the speaker telling you something is true? Telling you to do something? Wondering if something might happen? Wishing it would? Greek has four main moods: indicative (fact), imperative (command), subjunctive (may or might) and optative (wish). Each has its own card below. An everyday example. “You are kind.” (a statement) “ Be kind!” (a command) “If you were kind…” (a possibility) “ May you always be kind.” (a wish) Same idea, four different moods. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Mood helps you tell what God says is true from what he tells us to do , and from what is offered as a possibility or prayed as a wish . Mixing these up causes great confusion. If you read a promise as a command, you may feel you must earn it. If you read a command as merely a wish, you may not take it seriously. Noticing the mood helps you receive each sentence as God meant it. Romans 5:1 Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. “We have peace” is a statement of fact (indicative). Paul is not urging us to work up peace; he tells us we already have it. Matthew 11:28 Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. “Come” is a command (imperative). “I will give” is a statement of what Christ will do. An invitation and a promise together. Mood tells you whether to believe it, obey it, or pray it.

Indicative The indicative is the verb form used for plain statements of what is true or what happened. In plain words. The indicative is the mood of fact (see Mood ). It states that something is, was or will be so. Most sentences in ordinary speech are indicative. Questions about facts also use it. If a verb is simply telling you something, it is almost certainly indicative. An everyday example. “The kettle is boiling.” “Grandma came on Tuesday.” “The train will leave at nine.” Each one simply tells you how things are, were or will be. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The great truths of the gospel are stated in the indicative. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” “I am the bread of life.” These are not suggestions or hopes. They are statements of fact from God. The Christian life is built first on these indicatives: on what God says is true about Christ and about those who belong to him. Only then come the commands (see Indicative and imperative together ). Romans 8:1 There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. “There is” states a fact. For the believer, condemnation is gone, now, not just one day. John 6:35 Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, “I am” is a statement about who Jesus is. Faith rests on facts like this. The gospel starts with God’s indicatives: what is true because of Christ.

Imperative The imperative is the verb form used to give a command or make a request. In plain words. The imperative is the mood of command (see Mood ). It tells someone to do something, or not to do something. In English the imperative usually has no subject written down; “you” is understood. Imperatives can be strong orders, kind invitations or humble requests. The setting tells you which. An everyday example. “ Shut the door.” (an order) “ Come in and sit down!” (a warm invitation) “ Pass the salt, please.” (a polite request) Why it matters when you read the Bible. The Bible is full of imperatives, and they are not all the same in tone. “Come to me” is a loving invitation. “Pray without ceasing” is a call to a whole way of life. “Be filled with the Spirit” is interesting: it is an imperative, yet it is passive (see Passive voice ). We are told to let the Spirit fill us, not to fill ourselves. God’s commands are good and must be obeyed, but in the gospel they come to people he has already loved and saved, and he gives the strength to obey. Matthew 11:28 Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. “Come” is an imperative, but it is an invitation of grace, followed by a promise. Ephesians 5:18 And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, Two imperatives: a negative one (“do not get drunk”) and a positive one (“be filled”). The second is passive: we yield to the Spirit’s filling. 1 Thessalonians 5:17 pray without ceasing, A short imperative calling for an ongoing habit of prayer. Every command of God is a good command, given to people he has made his own.

Subjunctive The subjunctive is the verb form used for what may, might or should happen, rather than what simply is. In plain words. The subjunctive is the mood of possibility (see Mood ). It is used for things that are not stated as plain fact: what could happen, what someone hopes or intends will happen, or what happens “if” something else does. In English you often see it after words like if , so that , that or lest , with helping words like may , might or should . An everyday example. “I am saving so that we may go on holiday.” (a purpose) “ If it should rain, take the umbrella.” (a possibility) Why it matters when you read the Bible. The subjunctive often shows God’s purpose or a condition. John 3:16 says God gave his Son so that believers “should not perish but have eternal life”: that is the goal of God’s gift. In 1 John 1:9 the subjunctive goes with “if”: if we confess, he is faithful to forgive. The “if” is not a doubt about God, who is always faithful. It is a doorway: whenever we come confessing, forgiveness is there. Note that the subjunctive does not mean something is unlikely; it simply is not stated as a plain fact. John 3:16 that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. “Should not perish” and “have” show the purpose of God’s giving. 1 John 1:9 If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. “If we confess” is a condition. God’s faithfulness is stated as a fact: “he is faithful”. 1 John 2:1 I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. “That you may not sin” shows John’s purpose. Then the comfort: if we do sin, Christ is our advocate. The subjunctive often reveals God’s purpose and opens the door of an invitation.

Optative The optative is a rare Greek verb form used to express a wish or a prayer, like “may it be so” or “may it never be”. In plain words. The optative is the mood of wishing (see Mood ). It is quite rare in the New Testament. English has no special form for it, so we use may : may God bless you . Paul’s famous strong “No!” is an optative: mē genoito , literally “may it not be!” Some English Bibles translate it “May it never be!” The ESV usually gives it as “By no means!” and once as “far be it from me”. An everyday example. “ May you have a happy birthday!” “ Heaven forbid! ” These are wishes, not statements of fact or commands. Why it matters when you read the Bible. When Paul asks a shocking question, such as “Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?”, he answers with this optative: “By no means!” It is the strongest way he knows to reject the idea, a cry of horror. Grace is never a licence to sin. Elsewhere the optative turns into prayer. In 1 Thessalonians 5:23 Paul prays, “may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely”. Notice that he expresses it as a wish, yet he then adds, “He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it” (5:24). Romans 6:2 By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it? “By no means” is Paul’s optative “may it not be!” He utterly rejects the idea that grace encourages sin. Romans 6:15 Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means! The same strong optative. Being under grace means being freed from sin, not freed to sin. 1 Thessalonians 5:23 Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, “May … sanctify” is an optative of prayer. Paul turns his wish for the church into a prayer to God. Paul’s optative “By no means!” is the Bible’s loud no to using grace as an excuse.

Infinitive An infinitive is the basic “to” form of a verb, like “to live” or “to love”, which names an action without saying who does it or when. In plain words. The infinitive is a verb in its plainest form. In English it usually comes with to : to run , to believe , to forgive . It does not tell you who is doing the action or when. Infinitives are very flexible. They can act like a noun (a naming word) and be the subject of a sentence, or they can show purpose: in order to . An everyday example. “ To swim is good exercise.” Here “to swim” acts like a noun. “I went out to buy milk.” Here “to buy” shows why I went. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Infinitives often carry big ideas in just two words. “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” Paul uses two infinitives as the subjects of his sentence: living and dying. His whole life is Christ, and even death is gain because it means being with Christ. In Philippians 1:23 he longs “to depart and be with Christ”. Infinitives can also show God’s purpose, as when Christ “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25). Philippians 1:21 For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. “To live” and “to die” are infinitives used as subjects. Paul names the whole of life and death and fills both with Christ. Philippians 1:23 My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. “To depart and be with Christ” names what Paul desires. Hebrews 7:25 since he always lives to make intercession for them. “To make intercession” shows the purpose of Christ’s risen life: he lives to pray for his people. Infinitives can pack a whole hope into a few words.

Participle A participle is an “-ing” or “-ed” form of a verb that works like a describing word or adds extra action to a sentence. In plain words. A participle is part verb and part describing word. In English it often ends in -ing ( singing , believing ) or -ed ( loved , justified ). It can describe a person ( a sleeping baby ) or tell you more about the main action: when, how or why it happens. Greek uses participles far more than English does, so translators often turn them into phrases with since , when or by . An everyday example. “ Whistling a tune, Grandpa washed the dishes.” The main action is washing; “whistling” tells you how he did it. “The broken vase lay on the floor.” Here “broken” describes the vase. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Participles often depend on a main verb (see Main verb ), and seeing that link can change how you read a verse. In Matthew 28:19 “baptizing” describes how disciples are made. In Ephesians 5:18 to 21 the command “be filled with the Spirit” is followed by a string of participles: addressing, singing, giving thanks, submitting. These show what a Spirit-filled life looks like. Romans 5:1 has a participle too: “since we have been justified”, which gives the ground for having peace with God. Matthew 28:19 Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, “Baptizing” is a participle describing how disciples are made. It hangs on the main command “make disciples”. Ephesians 5:19 addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, A chain of participles flowing from “be filled with the Spirit” (5:18). Spirit-filled people sing and encourage one another. Romans 5:1 Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God “Since we have been justified” translates a participle. It gives the reason we have peace. Ask what a participle is hanging on, and you will often find the shape of the whole sentence.

Main verb The main verb is the chief action word in a sentence, the one the rest of the sentence leans on. In plain words. Long sentences can have many verbs, but usually one is the backbone. That is the main verb. The other verb forms, such as participles (see Participle ) or infinitives (see Infinitive ), add detail around it. To find the main verb, ask: “What is the one thing this sentence says someone does, or is?” Take away the extra bits and see what is left standing. An everyday example. “ Having finished her tea and putting on her coat, Mary went home.” The main verb is “went”. The rest just tells you what happened before she left. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Finding the main verb helps you see what a passage is really about. In the Great Commission the only command in the Greek is “make disciples”. “Go”, “baptizing” and “teaching” are participles that serve it. (Here “Go” still carries the force of a command alongside the main verb, which is why English Bibles rightly translate it “Go”.) So the heart of the mission is making disciples, and going, baptising and teaching are how it is done. In long letters like Paul’s, finding the main verb can stop you from getting lost in the details. Matthew 28:19 Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them “Make disciples” is the main verb. “Go” and “baptizing” are participles in Greek that serve the main command. Ephesians 5:18 but be filled with the Spirit, “Be filled” is the main command. The participles in verses 19 to 21 all flow from it. Romans 12:2 Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, Two main verbs, a “do not” and a “do”. The rest of the verse explains how and why. Find the main verb, and you find the backbone of the sentence.

Indicative and imperative together In the Bible, statements of what God has done (indicatives) usually come first, and commands about what we should do (imperatives) are built on them. In plain words. An indicative is a statement of fact (see Indicative ). An imperative is a command (see Imperative ). Throughout the New Testament these two come in a particular order: first what God has done for us in Christ, then what we are to do in response. Words like therefore and then often join them. This is sometimes called the “gospel pattern”: we obey because we have been saved, not in order to be saved. An everyday example. A father says, “You are a member of this family. So come and help set the table.” The child does not help in order to join the family. The child helps because he already belongs. Why it matters when you read the Bible. This pattern guards the heart of the gospel. Colossians 3 begins, “If then you have been raised with Christ” (a fact), and then commands, “seek the things that are above”. A few verses later: “Put to death therefore what is earthly in you”. In Ephesians Paul spends three chapters on what God has done, and then says, “I therefore … urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called”. If you take the commands without the facts, the Christian life becomes a crushing burden. If you take the facts without the commands, you miss the new life they produce. Keep them together, and in that order. Colossians 3:1 If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, First the fact (“you have been raised with Christ”), then the command (“seek the things that are above”). Colossians 3:5 Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: The “therefore” points back to what is true: you have died and your life is hidden with Christ (3:3). The command grows from that fact. Ephesians 4:1 I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called, “Therefore” links Paul’s appeal to chapters 1 to 3. We walk worthy of a calling God has already given. We obey because we have been saved, never in order to be saved.

Therefore “Therefore” tells you that what comes next follows from what was just said. In plain words. Some small words work like hinges on a door. They join one thought to another and show how the two belong together. “Therefore” is one of the most important. It means “because of all that, this follows”. Whenever you meet it, it points you back to what came before. Bible teachers like to say: when you see a “therefore”, ask what it is there for. An everyday example. “It is raining, therefore take your umbrella.” The umbrella only makes sense because of the rain. Take away the first half and the second half hangs in the air. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Paul often spends whole chapters telling us what God has done, then says “therefore” and tells us how to live. Romans 12:1 comes after eleven chapters of God’s mercy in the gospel. The call to give ourselves to God is not a way to earn his love. It is the thankful answer to love already given. Look back before you look forward. The order is always grace first, then obedience. Romans 12:1 I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice The “therefore” looks back over Romans 1 to 11. “The mercies of God” described there are the reason for the call to live for him. Romans 8:1 There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. This “therefore” gathers up what Paul has said about Christ’s saving work. Freedom from condemnation follows from what Christ has done, not from what we do. Romans 5:1 Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Peace with God is the result of being justified (declared right with God) by faith, which Paul has just explained in chapters 3 and 4. Asking what a “therefore” is there for keeps you from reading a command without the grace that comes before it.

For and because “For” and “because” give the reason for something. In plain words. When “for” stands at the start of a part of a sentence, it often means “because”. It answers the question “Why?” In older English, and in many Bible translations, “for” is used this way much more than in everyday speech today. So when you meet a “for” in the Bible, try reading it as “because” and see whether it fits. An everyday example. “I stayed at home, for I was ill.” This means “I stayed at home because I was ill.” The second half explains the first. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Reasons are the backbone of an argument. In Romans 1:16 Paul says he is not ashamed of the gospel, and then gives the reason: for it is God’s power to save. Verse 17 begins with another “for”, giving the reason why it is God’s power. Following these “for”s is like following footprints: each one shows you why the step before it is true. If you skip them, you get Paul’s conclusions without his reasons, and the reasons are often the most comforting part. Romans 1:16 For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes The second “for” means “because”. Paul is not ashamed of the gospel because it is God’s own power to save. Romans 6:23 For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. The opening “for” gives the reason behind what Paul has just said about the end of sin and the gift of God. Reading “for” as “because” lets you follow the reasons behind what the Bible says.

But “But” shows a turn: what comes next is different from, or against, what came before. In plain words. “But” is a turning word. It warns you that the sentence is about to change direction. What follows is a contrast: something different, unexpected, or opposite. Often the most important part of the sentence comes after the “but”. An everyday example. “The shop was closed, but the baker opened the door for me.” The first half sounds like bad news. The “but” turns it into good news. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Some of the greatest moments in the Bible turn on this small word. In Ephesians 2:1 to 3 Paul describes us as spiritually dead, following sin, and under God’s anger. Then comes verse 4: “But God”. Everything changes because God acted. When you read a “but”, pause and ask: what is being contrasted with what? You will often find the gospel in the gap between the two sides. Ephesians 2:4 But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, After three verses of bad news about our sin, “But God” turns everything around. Our rescue depends on God’s mercy, not on us. Romans 6:23 For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. The “but” sets two things side by side: what sin pays (death) and what God gives freely (eternal life). Proverbs 15:1 A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. Here “but” sets a wise way beside a foolish one, so that you see each more clearly. A “but” often marks the place where the Bible turns from our need to God’s answer.

So that (purpose) “So that” or “in order that” often tells you the purpose of something: what it is for. In plain words. Some joining words tell you the aim or goal behind an action. “So that”, “in order that”, and sometimes just “to”, answer the question “What for?” This is called purpose . It tells you what someone intends to happen. (The same words can also tell you what actually happened as a result; see Result .) An everyday example. “I set my alarm early so that I would catch the train.” Catching the train is the reason I set the alarm. It is my purpose. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Purpose words show you God’s intentions. John tells us why he wrote his Gospel: so that we may believe, and believing, have life. Paul tells us why Christ was made sin for us: so that we might become righteous in him. Spotting these words helps you see not only what God did but why he did it. It also guards you from reading a verse as a bare fact when it is really a loving aim. John 20:31 but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name. John states his purpose plainly. His Gospel was written so that readers would believe in Jesus and have life. 2 Corinthians 5:21 For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. “So that” shows God’s purpose in the cross: Christ took our sin in order that we might receive his righteousness. Galatians 2:16 so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law “In order to” gives the purpose of believing: to be put right with God by faith, not by keeping the law. Purpose words reveal not just what God has done but why he did it.

Result A result word tells you what actually happened because of something else. In plain words. Purpose is what someone aims at. Result is what actually comes about. In English we often use the same words for both, especially “so that” and “so … that”. You have to look at the sense to know which is meant. If you can put in “with the result that”, it is probably a result. An everyday example. “It rained all night, so that the river burst its banks.” Nobody planned the flood. It simply happened because of the rain. That is a result, not a purpose. Or: “She was so tired that she fell asleep at the table.” Why it matters when you read the Bible. Telling result from purpose can sharpen your reading. In Mark 4:37 the boat filling with water is plainly a result of the storm, not anyone’s goal. In John 3:16 many teachers point out that the words “so loved the world, that he gave” describe how God’s love showed itself: his love was such that it resulted in the gift of his Son. The word “so” there means “in this way” as much as “so much”. Translations cannot always show the difference, so a good commentary can help when it matters. Mark 4:37 And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. Here “so that” means “with the result that”. The filling boat is what happened because of the waves.
