John 3:16 For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son The “so … that” shows how God’s love worked out in action: it resulted in the giving of his only Son. Seeing whether a word marks purpose or result helps you tell what someone intended from what simply followed.

If … then (conditions) An “if” sentence says that one thing depends on another. In plain words. An “if” sentence has two halves. The “if” half sets up a situation. The second half, sometimes starting with “then”, tells you what follows in that situation. This is called a condition . Some “if”s are real questions: maybe yes, maybe no. But some “if”s speak about something that is certainly true. Then “if” comes close to meaning “since”. An everyday example. “ If it is sunny tomorrow, we will go to the beach.” Nobody knows yet whether it will be sunny. But a mother might say: “ If you are my child, you can come home any time.” She is not doubting it. She means “since you are my child”. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Many Bible “if”s are of the second kind. In Colossians 3:1 Paul is not doubting whether believers have been raised with Christ. He has just said they have (Colossians 2:12). The Greek here assumes it is true, so it is fair to hear “since”. That turns the verse from a test into an encouragement. Other “if”s, like 1 John 1:9, are true conditions: forgiveness is promised to those who confess. Ask each time: is this “if” a doubt or a “since”? Colossians 3:1 If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above This “if” assumes the fact. Since you have been raised with Christ, set your heart on heaven. 1 John 1:9 If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. A real condition with a sure promise: when we confess, God will certainly forgive, because he is faithful. Romans 8:31 If God is for us, who can be against us? Paul has just shown that God is for his people, so this “if” means “since”. The question that follows expects the answer “no one”. Some “if”s set a condition and some mean “since”: telling them apart can turn a worry into an assurance.

Although “Although” or “though” admits something is true and then says something surprising alongside it. In plain words. “Although” (or “though”, “even though”) introduces something that you would expect to stop what follows, yet it does not. Grammarians call this a concession , because the speaker concedes, or admits, one thing before saying something that seems to go against it. An everyday example. “ Although he was tired, he stayed up to help his friend.” Tiredness should have sent him to bed. It did not. The “although” makes his kindness stand out. Why it matters when you read the Bible. “Although” often shows us the wonder of Christ. Philippians 2:6 says that though he was in the form of God, he did not cling to his rights but humbled himself. Hebrews 5:8 says that although he was the Son, he learned obedience through suffering. In both, the “although” makes us marvel: the one who had every right to glory chose the path of humility for our sake. Philippians 2:6 who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, “Though” admits Christ’s full divine glory, and then shows the surprise: he did not hold on to it but humbled himself. Hebrews 5:8 Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered. Being God’s Son might seem to rule out suffering. The “although” shows that he truly entered into suffering as one of us. An “although” often points to grace: something done that need not have been done.

Just as (comparison) “Just as” or “as” compares two things, often to show the pattern or the reason for something. In plain words. “As” and “just as” set two things side by side and say they are alike in some way. This is called a comparison . In the Bible, “as” often does more than compare. It can also give the model to follow, and sometimes the reason: “do this, as (because) God has done this for you”. An everyday example. “Make the cake just as Grandma did.” Grandma’s cake is the pattern. You copy what she did. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Paul often grounds our behaviour in what God has done, using “as”. We forgive others as God in Christ forgave us. Husbands love their wives as Christ loved the church. The “as” gives both the measure (how much) and the motive (why). We do not forgive in order to be forgiven. We forgive because we have been forgiven, and Christ’s love shows us what love looks like. Ephesians 4:32 Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you. “As” gives both pattern and reason. Our forgiveness of others copies, and flows from, God’s forgiveness of us. Ephesians 5:25 Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, Christ’s self-giving love is the model. The “as” sets a high standard and points to the source of such love. An “as” in a command often points you to what God has already done for you.

Until “Until” marks the point up to which something lasts. In plain words. “Until” tells you how long something goes on: up to a certain time or event. In everyday speech it often suggests that things change afterwards. In the Bible, though, “until” usually focuses on the time leading up to the event. It does not always mean that what was happening stops afterwards. You need the rest of Scripture to tell you that. An everyday example. “Wait here until I come back.” You wait up to the moment I return. Whether you stay or leave afterwards depends on other things. Why it matters when you read the Bible. “Until” gives Christians a sense of waiting with hope. In the Lord’s Supper we proclaim Christ’s death “until he comes”: each Supper looks forward to his return. 1 Corinthians 15:25 says Christ must reign until all his enemies are under his feet. That does not mean his reign then ends. Scripture says elsewhere that his kingdom will have no end (Luke 1:33). So read “until” carefully, and let other passages fill out what happens afterwards. 1 Corinthians 11:26 For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. “Until he comes” makes the Lord’s Supper a meal of hope. It points forward to Christ’s return. 1 Corinthians 15:25 For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. “Until” marks the goal of Christ’s present reign. It does not mean his rule stops afterwards, since his kingdom has no end. Psalm 110:1 The LORD says to my Lord: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool.” The waiting time is marked by “until”. Christ is seated now, and the full victory over his enemies is sure. “Until” teaches us to live in the waiting time with hope, without assuming that what it describes must then stop.

Lists and the word “and” Sometimes the Bible repeats “and”, “or” or “nor” in a list to slow you down and make each item count. In plain words. Normally we write a list with commas and put “and” only before the last item. But a writer may repeat “and” (or “or”, or “nor”) between every item. This has a long name, polysyndeton , which simply means “many joinings”. It makes you slow down and feel each item. Leaving out the joining words altogether does the opposite: it makes the list rush by. An everyday example. Compare: “We packed bread, cheese, apples and water.” with “We packed bread and cheese and apples and water.” The second sounds fuller, as if every single thing mattered. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Hebrew writers joined almost everything with “and”, so in the Old Testament it is often just normal style. But in places, especially in Paul, the repetition is deliberate. In Romans 8:30 every “and those whom” links one of God’s acts to the next, like an unbreakable chain from before time to glory. In Romans 8:38 to 39 the long string of “nor”s piles up every possible threat, so that we feel how nothing at all can separate us from God’s love. Romans 8:30 And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified. Each “and” adds a link to the chain. No one drops out between one link and the next: God finishes what he starts. Romans 8:38 For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, The repeated “nor” names threat after threat, so that the final promise in verse 39 lands with full weight. Romans 8:35 Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? The repeated “or” makes us feel each trial in turn, and none of them can separate us from Christ’s love. A slow, repeated “and” or “nor” invites you to weigh each item, not skim past them.

Original languages The Bible was first written in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, and every English Bible is a translation. In plain words. Most of the Old Testament was written in Hebrew, with a few chapters in Aramaic, a related language. The New Testament was written in Greek, the common language of the Roman world. Every language works differently. Words do not match one for one, and word order and grammar differ. So translators must make choices, and that is why English Bibles do not all read the same. An everyday example. Try putting a simple French phrase into English. “Il fait froid” is word for word “it makes cold”, but in good English we say “it is cold”. A translator has to choose between closeness to the words and natural English. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Some translations stay close to the original wording. Others aim more at the general meaning in natural English. The ESV, used in this commentary, is “essentially literal”: it tries to keep the wording and structure of the original as far as good English allows. This is why it sometimes sounds a little formal. You do not need Greek or Hebrew to read the Bible well. God’s word comes through faithfully in good translations. But knowing that a translation is a translation helps you understand why footnotes and commentaries sometimes mention the original words. 2 Timothy 3:16 All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, “Breathed out by God” translates one Greek word. The ESV keeps its vivid picture: Scripture comes from God’s own breath, so faithful translations carry his word to us. John 1:1 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. “Word” translates the Greek logos . A single English word cannot hold all its meaning, which is one reason commentaries explain such terms. Knowing that your Bible is a careful translation helps you value it and understand why footnotes and commentaries sometimes look at the original words.

Genitive (“of”) The genitive is the Greek form often translated with “of”, and it can link two words in more than one way. In plain words. In English we join two nouns (naming words) with “of”: “the love of God”. Greek does this by changing the ending of the second noun. This form is called the genitive . The tricky thing is that “of” can mean different things. In “the love of God”, is God the one who loves (God loves us)? Or is God the one who is loved (we love God)? Scholars call the first a subjective genitive and the second an objective genitive. An everyday example. “ The fear of the lion was great.” Did the lion feel afraid, or were people afraid of the lion? The words alone do not say. Only the rest of the story tells you. Why it matters when you read the Bible. In 2 Corinthians 5:14, “the love of Christ” is usually taken as Christ’s love for us, because the verse goes on to speak of his death for all. But some think Paul also includes our love for Christ. A well-known debate is about “faith in Jesus Christ” in Galatians 2:16. The ESV footnote gives another possible reading, and some scholars take it as Christ’s own faithfulness. Many Reformed teachers keep “faith in Christ”. Either way, the verse clearly says that we are justified through Christ and not by works. When a commentary discusses an “of”, this is usually why. 2 Corinthians 5:14 For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all “The love of Christ” most likely means Christ’s love for us, shown in his death. That love is what drives Paul on. Galatians 2:16 yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ The Greek “of” here can be read as “faith in Jesus Christ” or “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ”. Both readings rest our salvation on Christ, not on our works. Romans 5:5 because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. Here context makes it plain: “God’s love” is God’s love for us, poured into our hearts by the Spirit. When a small “of” can be read two ways, the context and the rest of Scripture guide the reading.

Possessive A possessive word shows whom something belongs to, like “my”, “your” or “his”. In plain words. Possessive words tell you who owns or belongs to what. In English these are words like my , your , his , her , our , their , mine , and the little ending ’s (as in “God’s word”). In Greek and Hebrew belonging is often shown with the genitive (see Genitive ) or with a small ending on the word. An everyday example. “This is my coat.” “That is Sarah’s bag.” The possessive word tells you whose they are. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Small possessive words carry great comfort. David does not just say “The LORD is a shepherd”. He says “my shepherd”. Jesus speaks of “my sheep” who hear “my voice”. The bride in the Song of Solomon says “My beloved is mine, and I am his”. These little words speak of belonging and personal relationship. The Heidelberg Catechism begins in the same spirit: our only comfort is that we belong to our faithful Saviour Jesus Christ. Notice the “my”s and “his”s, and receive them personally. Psalm 23:1 The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. “My” makes the LORD’s care personal. Because he is my shepherd, I shall lack nothing I truly need. John 10:27 My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. Jesus’ “my” shows that his people belong to him, and his voice is the voice they know. Song of Solomon 2:16 My beloved is mine, and I am his Belonging runs both ways: “mine” and “his”. Christians have long heard here an echo of the bond between Christ and his people. A small “my” in the Bible often turns a general truth into a personal comfort.

Gender in grammar Some languages use male words in a general way that includes women too, such as “brothers” or “man”. In plain words. In Greek, Hebrew and older English, a group of men and women together is usually described with the male form of a word. So “brothers” (Greek adelphoi ) can mean “brothers and sisters” when the whole church is addressed. Likewise “man” can mean “human beings”. This is a feature of the language, not a sign that women are left out. An everyday example. In older English, a teacher might say “Every pupil must bring his book”, meaning both boys and girls. Or a sign might say “ Man has walked on the moon”, meaning the human race. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The ESV keeps “brothers” in the text, but adds a footnote in many places explaining that the word can refer to both men and women who are members of God’s family. When Paul writes to the church in Philippi or Thessalonica, he speaks to the sisters as well as the brothers. And when Jesus quotes “Man shall not live by bread alone”, it applies to every person. Sometimes, though, the context shows that only men are meant, so read each case carefully. Philippians 3:1 Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. “Brothers” here addresses the whole church, men and women. The ESV footnotes on this word explain that it can include both. 1 Thessalonians 4:13 But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep This comfort about believers who have died is for every Christian, sister and brother alike. Matthew 4:4 Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God. “Man” here means any human being. All of us need God’s word as truly as we need food. Knowing how “brothers” and “man” are used helps every reader hear the Bible speaking to them.

Hebrew parallelism Parallelism is the way Hebrew poetry says something in one line and then echoes, contrasts or builds on it in the next. In plain words. English poems often rhyme sounds. Hebrew poems “rhyme” ideas. A line says something, and the next line answers it. Sometimes the second line says nearly the same thing in other words. Sometimes it says the opposite, often joined by “but”. Sometimes it takes the thought one step further. This pairing of lines is called parallelism , and it is found all through the Psalms, Proverbs and the Prophets. An everyday example. “The sun was warm; the day was bright.” (the same idea twice) “The lazy man sleeps; the busy man prospers.” (a contrast) “He walked to the door, he opened it, he stepped outside.” (building up step by step) Why it matters when you read the Bible. Parallelism helps you understand each line by the other. In Psalm 119:105 “lamp to my feet” and “light to my path” explain each other. In Proverbs 15:1 the contrast between a soft answer and a harsh word makes the lesson clear. In Psalm 1:1 the man who is blessed does not walk, stand or sit with the wicked: each step goes further in. Isaiah 53:5 piles up line after line about Christ’s suffering for us. Do not try to find a separate meaning for every echoing line. Let the lines work together. Psalm 119:105 Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path. The same idea twice: “lamp” and “light”, “feet” and “path”. God’s word shows us the way step by step. Proverbs 15:1 A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. A contrast: the two lines are opposites, joined by “but”, so the wise way stands out. Psalm 1:1 Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers; Building up: walking, then standing, then sitting. Each line shows a deeper settling into sin. Reading the lines of Hebrew poetry together lets each one explain the other.

Chiasm A chiasm is a mirror pattern, where ideas are given in one order and then repeated in reverse. In plain words. A chiasm (say “KY-asm”) is a pattern like A, B, then B, A. The second half mirrors the first. The name comes from the Greek letter chi , which looks like an X, because if you draw lines between the matching parts they cross. Sometimes a chiasm is just two lines long. Sometimes it covers a whole passage, and then the middle point is often the most important. An everyday example. “Eat to live, don’t live to eat.” Eat (A), live (B), live (B), eat (A). The mirror makes the saying stick in the mind. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Mirror patterns make sayings memorable and sharp. In Mark 2:27 Jesus says the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath: the reversal shows what the Sabbath is for. Matthew 23:12 mirrors exalting and humbling to show God’s great reversal. Genesis 9:6 mirrors blood and man to show that the punishment fits the crime. Be a little careful: some people find chiasms everywhere. A real one is usually clear once it is pointed out. Mark 2:27 The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Sabbath, man, man, Sabbath. The mirror shows that God gave the Sabbath as a gift for people, not a burden over them. Matthew 23:12 Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. Exalts, humbled, humbles, exalted. The crossing pattern pictures God turning human pride upside down. Genesis 9:6 Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed Sheds, blood, man, then man, blood, shed. The mirror shows that the penalty matches the crime, because people bear God’s image. Spotting a mirror pattern helps you see what a saying stresses and where a passage’s centre lies.

Inclusio (bookends) An inclusio is when a passage begins and ends with the same words, like bookends on a shelf. In plain words. Writers sometimes start and finish a section with the same phrase or idea. This is called an inclusio (a Latin word meaning “shutting in”). It works like bookends: it shows where a section begins and ends, and it tells you what the whole section is about. An everyday example. A speech might begin, “Thank you all for coming,” and end, “Again, thank you all for coming.” The repeated words frame everything in between and show what the speaker most wanted to say. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Psalm 8 begins and ends with the same line: “O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!” Everything in between, even the wonder of human beings, is framed by the majesty of God. Psalm 103 begins and ends with “Bless the LORD, O my soul”. Once you notice these frames, you see the theme of the whole passage. In longer passages, a repeated phrase can mark off a section that belongs together, which helps you avoid lifting a verse out of its setting. Psalm 8:1 O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth! The psalm opens with God’s majesty. Psalm 8:9 O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth! It closes with exactly the same words. The whole psalm, including its praise of humanity, is framed by God’s glory. Psalm 103:22 Bless the LORD, O my soul! The psalm ends where it began (verse 1). All the reasons for praise in between are held inside this call to worship. Bookends show you where a passage starts and stops, and what it is mainly about.

Repetition for emphasis Saying a word two or three times in a row is a way of underlining it. In plain words. We underline or use bold type to stress a word. Hebrew and Greek had no bold type, so one way to stress something was to repeat it. Saying a word twice makes it strong. Saying it three times makes it as strong as it can be. An everyday example. A parent might say, “Be careful, careful, careful on that ladder!” Or a child might shout, “It’s very, very, very big!” The repetition shows how much it matters. Why it matters when you read the Bible. In Isaiah 6:3 the angels cry “Holy, holy, holy”. This rare threefold repetition shows how utterly holy he is. Jesus often begins with “Truly, truly, I say to you” (in older Bibles “Verily, verily”). It is his solemn way of saying: listen carefully, this is certainly true. When you meet a repeated word, slow down. The Bible is underlining it for you. Isaiah 6:3 Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory! The threefold “holy” stresses God’s holiness as strongly as possible. John 3:3 Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God. The double “truly” marks a solemn, certain truth: the new birth is necessary to enter God’s kingdom. When the Bible repeats a word, it is underlining something you should not miss.

The prophetic perfect The prophetic perfect is when a prophet speaks of a future event as if it had already happened, because God has made it certain. In plain words. Hebrew verbs do not show time in quite the same way English does. One verb form usually describes a completed action, and is often translated with the past tense. Yet prophets sometimes use this “completed” form for things still in the future. Scholars call this the prophetic perfect . It speaks of the future as already done, because in God’s plan it is as good as done. An everyday example. Imagine a father who has bought his son a bicycle for his birthday next week. He might say, “You’ve got a new bike!” The gift is so certain that he speaks as if it has already arrived. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Isaiah 9 and Isaiah 53 were written centuries before Christ. Yet Isaiah says “to us a child is born” and “he was pierced for our transgressions”. The prophet sees the coming Saviour so surely that he speaks as if it has already happened. This should strengthen our confidence in God’s promises. A word of care: not every past tense in the prophets is a prophetic perfect, and scholars sometimes disagree about particular verses. Hebrew verbs are complex, and a good commentary will help. Isaiah 9:6 For to us a child is born, to us a son is given Written long before Christ’s birth, yet spoken as already done. God’s promise of the Messiah was certain. Isaiah 53:5 But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities Isaiah describes the suffering of the Servant as finished, centuries before the cross, because God had determined it. Isaiah 9:2 The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light The light of the coming King is spoken of as already seen. Matthew 4:16 shows it was fulfilled in Jesus. When God promises something, it is so sure that his prophets could speak of it as already done.

Hebrew names that carry meaning In the Bible a name often has a meaning that tells you something about the person or about God’s purpose. In plain words. Most English names today are chosen because they sound nice. In Bible times names often meant something. A name could describe a person, remember an event, or announce a promise. When God changed someone’s name, it marked a new calling. Footnotes in the ESV often explain what a name means. An everyday example. Some English names still carry meaning: “Joy”, “Grace” or “Hope”. If you met a girl called Hope, born after a long hard time, you would understand why her parents chose it. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Bible writers often explain names for us, so watch for “which means” or “for”. “Abram” means “exalted father”, and God renamed him “Abraham”, which sounds like “father of a multitude”, because of his promise. “Jesus” is the Greek form of “Joshua”, meaning “the LORD saves”: so the angel says “you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins”. “Immanuel” means “God with us”. These names preach the gospel in a single word. Matthew 1:21 you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins. The name Jesus means “the LORD saves”. The “for” explains it: he is named for what he came to do. Matthew 1:23 and they shall call his name Immanuel” (which means, God with us). Matthew translates the Hebrew name for us. In Jesus, God himself has come to be with his people. Genesis 17:5 No longer shall your name be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham, for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations. God’s new name for Abraham carries his promise. Every time he heard his name, he was reminded of it. A Bible name is often a small sermon about who someone is and what God will do.

Literal and figurative Literal words mean exactly what they say; figurative words use a picture to say something true in another way. In plain words. When we speak literally , the words mean just what they say. When we speak figuratively , we use a picture, a comparison or an image to make a point. A figure of speech is not untrue. It is a way of telling the truth vividly. Reformed teachers have always said we should read the Bible “literally” in the right sense: according to the kind of writing it is, and what the author meant, including his figures of speech. An everyday example. “It’s raining cats and dogs!” Nobody looks for animals falling from the sky. Everyone understands it means very heavy rain. That is figurative. “It is raining hard” says the same thing literally. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Jesus often spoke figuratively, and people sometimes misunderstood him. When he told Nicodemus he must be “born again”, Nicodemus took it literally and asked how a grown man could enter his mother’s womb. Jesus meant a new birth by the Spirit. When Jesus says “I am the door”, he is not made of wood. He is the only way into God’s salvation. Ask what kind of language you are reading. Figures are not less true; they are often more memorable. John 3:4 How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born? Nicodemus takes “born again” literally. Jesus meant a spiritual new birth, and the misunderstanding helps explain his meaning. John 10:9 I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved A figurative picture. Jesus is the one way into safety and life with God. Telling literal from figurative language helps you hear what the author truly means.

Metaphor A metaphor says one thing is another thing, to show what they have in common. In plain words. A metaphor is a picture made with words. Instead of saying something is like something else (see Simile ), it simply says it is that thing. We know it is not meant literally, but the picture helps us see a truth more clearly. An everyday example. “My grandson is a ray of sunshine .” He is not really sunlight. But he brightens the day and warms your heart. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The Bible is full of metaphors for God and for Christ. “The LORD is my rock” speaks of his strength and reliability. “I am the vine; you are the branches” shows how closely believers are joined to Christ and depend on him for life and fruit. When you meet a metaphor, ask: in what ways is this picture true? Think about rocks, fortresses, vines and branches. But do not push every detail too far. A metaphor usually makes one or a few main points. Psalm 18:2 The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer God is not literally a rock or a castle, but these pictures show he is strong, steady and safe to hide in. John 15:5 I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. The vine and branches picture our total dependence on Christ. Cut off from him, a branch bears nothing. Metaphors let you see and feel truths about God that plain statements alone might leave abstract.

Simile A simile compares two things using “like” or “as”. In plain words. A simile is a close cousin of a metaphor (see Metaphor ). The difference is that a simile says openly that it is making a comparison, using “like” or “as”. It tells you one thing is like another in some way. An everyday example. “He eats like a horse.” “She is as busy as a bee.” The words “like” and “as” show that a comparison is being made. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Similes help you picture spiritual truths. Psalm 1:3 says the godly person is like a tree planted by streams of water: rooted, nourished and fruitful. Isaiah 53:6 says we all like sheep have gone astray: foolish, wandering and helpless. Psalm 42:1 compares longing for God with a thirsty deer. Ask what the two things share. The picture often carries both a warning and a comfort. Psalm 1:3 He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season The godly person is compared to a well-watered tree: steady, fed and fruitful, because he delights in God’s word. Isaiah 53:6 All we like sheep have gone astray The simile shows our wandering and helplessness, and prepares for the good news that the LORD laid our sin on his Servant. Psalm 42:1 As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God. “As … so” compares deep thirst with the soul’s longing for God. A simile invites you to picture one thing in order to understand another.

Hyperbole (exaggeration) Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration to make a point strongly. In plain words. Hyperbole (say “hy-PER-bo-lee”) is when someone overstates something on purpose. It is not lying, because everyone understands it is not meant to be taken word for word. It is a way of making a point so strongly that you cannot miss it. An everyday example. “I’ve told you a thousand times !” “I’m so hungry I could eat a horse .” Nobody counts to a thousand or eats a horse. The exaggeration shows how strongly the speaker feels. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Jesus used hyperbole to wake people up. He told his hearers to tear out an eye that causes sin. He did not mean self-harm, for the sin comes from the heart, not the eye. He meant: deal with sin ruthlessly. In Luke 14:26 he says a disciple must “hate” his family. Matthew 10:37 shows the meaning: love Christ more than anyone else. To read hyperbole woodenly misses the point. To explain it away also misses the point. Feel its force: following Christ is worth more than anything. Matthew 5:29 If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. Jesus is not commanding self-harm. The shocking picture shows how seriously we must fight sin. Luke 14:26 If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. “Hate” is a strong exaggeration meaning “love less by comparison” (compare Matthew 10:37). Christ must come first. Matthew 19:24 it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God. A deliberately impossible picture. Salvation is impossible for us, but as verse 26 says, with God all things are possible. Hyperbole is meant to shake us, not to be taken word for word nor brushed aside.

Idiom An idiom is a fixed phrase whose meaning is different from the meaning of its separate words. In plain words. Every language has phrases that cannot be understood just by adding up the words. These are called idioms . People who grow up with the language know what they mean. People from outside are often puzzled. The Bible, written in Hebrew and Greek, has idioms too, and translators must decide whether to keep them word for word or put the meaning in plain English. An everyday example. “He kicked the bucket ” means “he died”. “She pulled my leg ” means “she was joking with me”. A foreign visitor might take them literally and be very confused. Why it matters when you read the Bible. In Genesis 4:1 “Adam knew Eve his wife” is a Hebrew idiom for married intimacy, which is why she then conceived. In Luke 9:51 Jesus “set his face” to go to Jerusalem: he was firmly determined, knowing the cross awaited him. In 1 Peter 1:13 the ESV says “preparing your minds for action”. The footnote gives the original idiom, “girding up the loins of your mind”, which pictures tucking up a long robe to run or work. Footnotes and commentaries help unlock idioms. Genesis 4:1 Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain “Knew” is a Hebrew idiom for the closest bond of marriage. It also suggests that this union is deeply personal. Luke 9:51 When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. “Set his face” means he was firmly resolved. Jesus went to the cross willingly, for us. 1 Peter 1:13 Therefore, preparing your minds for action, and being sober-minded, set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you The ESV turns a picture idiom (literally “girding up the loins of your mind”) into plain English: get your mind ready. Knowing an idiom means knowing what the phrase meant to its first hearers, not just what its words say.

Personification Personification describes a thing or an idea as if it were a person who can speak, feel or act. In plain words. Personification gives human qualities to something that is not human: a river, a hill, the sea, or an idea like wisdom. It lets us feel the truth in a lively way. It does not mean the thing is really a person. An everyday example. “The wind howled all night.” “The old house groaned in the storm.” Wind does not howl like a wolf and houses do not groan like people, but the words help you hear and feel the scene. Why it matters when you read the Bible. In Proverbs 8 wisdom calls out in the streets like a woman inviting people to listen. This makes God’s wisdom warm and urgent. In Psalm 98 rivers clap their hands and hills sing for joy at the coming of the Lord. All creation joins the praise. In Romans 8:22 creation groans like a woman in labour, waiting for its renewal. Personification helps us feel how the whole world is caught up in God’s story of judgment and salvation. Proverbs 8:1 Does not wisdom call? Does not understanding raise her voice? Wisdom is pictured as a woman calling aloud. God’s wisdom is not hidden; it invites everyone to listen. Psalm 98:8 Let the rivers clap their hands; let the hills sing for joy together Rivers and hills are pictured as worshippers. All creation rejoices at the coming of the LORD. Romans 8:22 For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. Creation is pictured as a woman in labour. Its pain is real, but it is the pain that comes before new birth. Personification helps us feel that all creation shares in God’s story.

Anthropomorphism Anthropomorphism describes God using human features, like hands, eyes or ears, to help us understand him. In plain words. The long word comes from two Greek words: anthropos , “human”, and morphe , “form”. It means speaking of God as if he had a human body. God is spirit (John 4:24) and has no body like ours. But he lovingly speaks to us in words we can understand. When the Bible speaks of his hand, it means his power. His eyes and ears mean that he sees and hears all. An everyday example. When we tell a small child “Grandpa has a big heart”, we do not mean his heart is physically large. We mean he is very loving. We use body words to describe what a person is like. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Reformed theologians, following Calvin, have spoken of God “accommodating” himself to us. Like a parent stooping to speak to a child, he uses simple pictures. “The LORD’s hand is not shortened” means he is never too weak to save. “The eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth” means he sees everything and is ready to help his people. Do not take these pictures as saying God has a body. Do not dismiss them either. They tell real truth about the living God. Isaiah 59:1 Behold, the LORD’s hand is not shortened, that it cannot save, or his ear dull, that it cannot hear; God’s “hand” stands for his power and his “ear” for his attention. He is always able to save and always hears. 2 Chronicles 16:9 For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him. God’s “eyes” picture his complete knowledge and his watchful care for those who trust him. John 4:24 God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth. This plain statement reminds us that God has no body. The body pictures elsewhere are figures of speech. Body words for God are his kindness in speaking our language, and they tell us true things about him.

Merism A merism names two opposite ends to mean everything in between. In plain words. A merism uses a pair of opposites to say “all of it”. By naming the two extremes, it includes everything between them. It is a short, vivid way of saying “everything” or “always” or “everywhere”. An everyday example. “I searched high and low for my keys.” This means I searched everywhere, not just on the top shelf and the floor. “She works day and night ” means she works all the time. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Genesis 1:1 says God created “the heavens and the earth”. Hebrew had no single word for “universe”, so this pair means everything that exists. In Psalm 139:2 “when I sit down and when I rise up” means all my activities: God knows everything I do. In Revelation 22:13 Christ is “the Alpha and the Omega” (the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet): he is the beginning and end of all things and everything between. Seeing a merism helps you grasp how large the claim is. Genesis 1:1 In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. “The heavens and the earth” means the whole universe. Nothing exists that God did not make. Psalm 139:2 You know when I sit down and when I rise up; you discern my thoughts from afar. Sitting down and rising up stand for all of life. God knows every part of it. Revelation 22:13 I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. Three merisms in a row. Christ is Lord over all of history, from start to finish. A merism uses two ends to say “all”, so it often makes a claim much larger than it first looks.

Euphemism A euphemism is a gentle way of speaking about something hard or delicate. In plain words. A euphemism replaces a harsh or awkward word with a softer one. We use euphemisms out of kindness, respect or modesty. The Bible does the same, especially when speaking of death and of private matters. An everyday example. Instead of “He died”, we may say “He passed away .” Instead of “toilet”, we may say “the bathroom ”. The meaning is clear, but the words are gentler. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The New Testament often speaks of the death of believers as “falling asleep”. This is more than politeness. It expresses Christian hope: sleep is followed by waking. Jesus said, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep”, and the disciples misunderstood, so he had to say plainly, “Lazarus has died.” Stephen, stoned for his faith, “fell asleep”. For those in Christ, death has lost its sting. The gentle word carries the promise of resurrection. John 11:11 Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him. Jesus speaks of death as sleep because he is about to raise Lazarus. For him, waking the dead is like waking a sleeper. John 11:14 Then Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus has died, When the disciples miss the euphemism, Jesus says it plainly. This shows that “asleep” really meant death. Acts 7:60 And when he had said this, he fell asleep. Stephen’s violent death is described with a gentle word. For a believer, death is a sleep from which Christ will awaken him. The Bible’s gentle words about the death of believers carry the sure hope of the resurrection.

Irony Irony is saying one thing while meaning, or showing, something quite different, often the opposite. In plain words. Irony comes in different kinds. Sometimes a speaker says the opposite of what he means, to make a point sharply. This is sometimes called sarcasm. Sometimes people say something that is truer than they realise, while the reader can see the real truth. This is called dramatic irony . An everyday example. Looking out at pouring rain, someone says, “ Lovely weather for a picnic!” They mean the opposite. Or in a story, a character says “Nothing can go wrong now”, while the reader knows the danger behind the door. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Paul uses irony with the proud Corinthians: “Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings!” He means they think they have arrived, but they have not. Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal: perhaps their god is asleep. The greatest irony is at the cross. The soldiers mock Jesus with “Hail, King of the Jews!” and Pilate writes the same title over his head. They meant it as a joke, but it was the truth. Missing irony can make you read a verse the wrong way round. 1 Corinthians 4:8 Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! Paul is being ironic. The Corinthians think they are spiritually rich and mature, but their pride shows the opposite. 1 Kings 18:27 Either he is musing, or he is relieving himself, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened. Elijah mocks Baal’s worshippers. The irony exposes that their god is nothing at all. Matthew 27:29 And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” Dramatic irony: the soldiers mean it as mockery, but Jesus truly is the King, reigning even from the cross. Spotting irony keeps you from reading a verse the wrong way round, and often shows the truth more sharply.
